### AI Cult
I've read several times that AI should lead companies, or even states. "Why do we need humans if AI can know much more than any human?" This is a dangerous kind of thinking.
I'm a big fan of AI, but at the end of the day, it's still just advanced statistics. It's a powerful tool, but if you train your model on unrepresentative, toxic, or otherwise improper data, you'll end up with a toxic and improper model.
The problem is that the datasets used to train models are often huge. It's difficult to ensure that the data is valid, representative, and free from toxicity or manipulation.
I see great potential in MCP and RAG. In the end, we don't need a model that knows everything. We need models that understand language and can work with external information. So it's not just about how much a model knows, but how well it can work with the added data. This approach can give better results, but data validity is still the bottleneck.

It sounds like two different personal qualities, but after thinking about it, I realized that my strength and weakness are actually the same: it's how I perceive time.

So, my strength is also my weakness.

### Náš zákazník, náš pán
Včera jsem byl na oslavě, kde jsem konečně po dvou letech mohl mluvit s "třídní důvěrnicí" ve škole, kam chodí moje dcera. Ta role ve škole vznikla jen kvůli té paní, která si to vydupala a zřizovatel na to kývnul. Náš zákazník, náš pán. Jenže problém je v tom, že paní byla toxická. Tu roli pojala tak, že šířila špatnou náladu. Výsledek byl, že naše třídní učitelka to psychicky nedala a odešla ze školy. Dokonce psala i dopis investorům školy, aby je odradila od dalších investic.  "Třídní důvěrnice" nakonec taky odešla, ale podařilo se ji otrávit zaměstnance a i některé rodiče. A to toxické myšlení šíří dál a vůbec se tím netají, že bude dále pomlouvat.
Na jednu stranu si člověk říká, že soukromá škola nemůže být ke klientům tvrdá. Však platí školné a tak umožňují existenci školy. Na druhou stranu na tomto názorném příkladu vidím, jakou paseku umí napáchat toxický klient.
K té roli třídního důvěrníka se dostala prostě tak, že si tu roli vymyslela, sama se nominovala a přesvědčila nějaké rodiče, aby ji dali hlas. Já tenkrát vůbec nehlasoval, protože ani s jedním kandidátem jsem si nikdy ani půl hodinu nepovídal a ani o nich nic nevěděl. Považoval jsem to od počátku za zbytečnou pozici, která vznikla jen proto, aby byla zákaznice uspokojena. Výsledek byl katastrofa.
Z toho pro mě plyne ponaučení, že zákazníkovi je třeba naslouchat, ale zároveň jasně nastavit limity. Toxický zákazník sice může krátkodobě přinést nějaké peníze, ale v dlouhodobém horizontu vás připraví o mnohem více.

Companies move fast to fix technical debt.
But what about culture debt?
We all know what technical debt looks like:
- Messy code that slows you down
- Quick fixes that cause bigger problems later
- A system that works… but barely
So companies invest time and energy to clean it up.
But there’s another kind of debt that’s quieter; and often way more dangerous:
Culture debt.
It shows up as:
❌ Teams that avoid hard conversations
❌ Blame instead of ownership
❌ Silos where no one shares knowledge
❌ New ideas getting shut down before they start
❌ Talented people leaving because they feel unheard
Just like tech debt, culture debt starts small.
A compromise here. A shortcut there.
But over time, it compounds until suddenly your best people are disengaged, innovation slows, and trust disappears.
And here’s the hard truth:
You can’t build great products on a broken culture.
So the question is:
👉🏾 Is your company paying down its culture debt or letting it pile up?
👉🏾 Are you investing in trust, communication, and shared purpose or only in code refactoring?
Because fixing culture debt isn’t optional.
It’s the foundation for any real, lasting progress.

Semantic search is the foundation of 𝗥𝗔𝗚 (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). All those AI chatbots use semantic search to retrieve relevant documents. It’s also useful as a search tool for your website. You can find articles by their meaning, not just by the words they contain.

### Sprint vs Long-Distance
There are two main types of runners: sprinters and long-distance runners. These types of runners are very different. They have different body types, different mentalities, and different strengths. Sprinters are usually bad at long distances, and long-distance runners aren't good sprinters.
Programmers are the same. Some of them are fast but get tired easily. Some are slower but can focus for a longer time. In IT, we often use tests as an "objective" measurement of a candidate, but these tests mainly assess how good of a sprinter you are. Yes, for some tasks it's necessary to write fast and simple functions, but I believe that most developer work involves long-distance tasks, where it’s not about how fast you can write a simple function, but how well you handle complexity.
Complexity isn't a sprint; it's a long-distance run. You have to think about things from different angles, look for weak points, and spot hidden details. This kind of thinking is exactly what slows us down in time-limited testing. Reason, why complex mind has lower performance in time-limited testing.

### We Have Valid Data
I've heard the same claim many times: "Our data is valid." But before I perform any migration or mass action, I always double-check the data. Truly valid data is something very rare in real life.
### What I’ve fund:
- Data from legacy systems that nobody understands anymore.
- Data from unrelated systems not connected to the website.
- Valid data stored in improper fields or columns.
- Stored XSS attempts and strangely formatted data
- Publicly visible test data in the production environment.
Once, I was working with a "tailored e-shop" and discovered that the database contained data and structures from another "tailored e-shop." The developers had reused an existing shop, changed some configurations, but left old, unrelated data in the new version.
Another example: I was importing data from Excel. It was a complex sheet with many columns, patterns, and hundreds of rows. No surprise—some data ended up in the wrong columns.
Migrations from legacy systems are always messy. Developers are often too lazy to validate data consistency and end up copying fields from deleted entities or including unused files.

### Is AI Code Insecure?
I’ve read several times that AI-generated code isn’t secure. But what is AI? When we say AI, we usually mean LLMs, which are based on statistics. This means they can reproduce insecure code—but only because they’ve seen it in certain repositories.
If I were a malicious hacker, I would create repositories with insecure code, spread links to them, and let scrapers find them. Then I’d hope that some model would pick up my insecure code and use it as a datasets for training.
What does this mean? It means that LLMs themselves aren’t insecure, but their datasets can be. This risk only emphasizes the importance of high-quality data sources. That’s the weak point—not the design of the LLM, but its knowledge sources.

# Can You Share? Sharing Is Caring! Or Not? What I Learned from OSINT
OSINT is short for Open Source Intelligence. It means retrieving information from public sources. Public sources include all types of media, social networks, catalogs, registers, websites, and much more. We are sharing information everywhere.
I used to have a public mobile phone. I mean, it’s still public, but that’s why I blocked all calls from unknown numbers. The first problem is spam; the second problem with a public phone is scammers. Anyone with basic IT skills can spoof any phone number. It’s not difficult, and it’s also not illegal. This means a scammer can call someone using your phone number (which is illegal). We can’t trust incoming calls. That’s why I’m hesitant to share my mobile phone publicly.
I have several email accounts. For sensitive services, I use a "secret email" that isn't publicly known. This adds an extra layer of security, making it harder to hack through social engineering or brute force.
For example, imagine you have an account on a service that exposes information publicly. We also know that spoofing a phone number isn’t difficult. Now, imagine your email and phone number are publicly available, and an attacker knows you have an account on a specific service. You receive a call from a number that appears to be associated with that company. To simplify, imagine you share information about your bank, and your phone number is public. Then, you receive a call from what looks like your bank, and the caller claims you need to take urgent action. This is a common spear-phishing attack.
When searching for a job or looking for candidates, sharing some information is necessary. However, we should always consider the risks we create by doing so.

Follow the pattern
I spent years practicing martial arts. I had different sifus/professors, trained in different styles, and experienced different cultural influences. I found that the teaching approach was always the same: don’t speak - just follow what your master does. If a student can reproduce the patterns, they will eventually understand their purpose. Programming, perhaps surprisingly, is similar to martial arts. You have to practice - again and again. You need to recognize patterns and follow them. In interviews, design patterns are a frequent topic, but I’m not sure if it’s necessary to understand every single one. A good programmer must be able to reproduce a pattern. Yes, if you understand a pattern, you can create it from scratch, but we live in a time where frameworks exist, and we don’t need to start every app from the ground up.
I believe the important part is understanding the pattern, being able to reproduce it, and knowing what it does. It’s not essential to know whether it’s called a singleton, MVC, builder, or factory. I know seniors with years of experience who aren’t able to do this. What’s more important is being able to apply the pattern effectively. Design patterns are useful when writing a new framework or transitioning between frameworks. However, in my view, the key isn’t being able to name the pattern - it’s being able to implement it.

Modern IDEs provide features that make memorizing documentation unnecessary because it's readily available within the IDE. However, without an IDE, my coding skills feel downgraded. In reality, I always use an IDE, so I don't need to memorize as much, and with an IDE, I work much faster.
In real life, we use many tools, which is good because they make us evolutionarily efficient. However, the job market still expects us to function without them. We now have tools more powerful than any human, yet we resist fully embracing them because we believe that everyone must first understand how they work to use them. But that isn't true—I have very limited knowledge of semiconductors, yet I use them every day.
We should ask ourselves whether humans are truly prepared for AI. I often read about AI's potential and how important it is for companies, but at the same time, I see "good old processes" still in place that don’t account for this new reality.

Konec retargetingu na Safari?  Jak to asi funguje?
Dle článku Safari blokuje scripty, které ukládají cookies třetích stran i vlastní cookies webu.  Pro blokaci má sloužit AI.
V případě Skliku to je celkem jasné. Sklik má vlastní retargetinový kód. Jenže Google AdWords používá retargetinové seznamy, které se vytváří na základě analytického kódu Universal Analytics. Což by mohlo znamenet, že buď Safari bude blokovat Universal  Analytics, nebo bude blokovat "jen" reklamy.
V prvním případě by jsme o data o uživatelích/návštěvách přišli, ve druhém bychom přišli pouze o možnost na základě těch dat inzerovat.
V prvním případě bychom mohli říct, že Apple (Safari) postavilo soukromí uživatelů nad zájmy provozovatelů webů (tzn. žádná data o návštěvnosti). V druhém případě by šlo jen určitý alibismus. Soukromí uživatelů by stále bylo narušeno, jen by z toho nikdo neměl přímý zisk.
Pokud jsem správně pochopil situaci, tak se jedná jen o ten druhý případ. Tedy že si Apple usmyslelo, že nechceme reklamu na míru. Což já osobně teda chci.  Soukromí nezískáme, jen ztratíme možnost dostávat obsah, který dostávat chceme. A kdo reklamy na míru nechce? AdBlock funguje už dlouho, takže v čem je problém?
